Forum posts also contained email address and password pairs belonging to other victims, bringing the total to 7.2M unique email addresses.

title: СберСпасибо (SberSpasibo) - 3,288,711 breached accounts

It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.”

Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily diaries, almost 100 notebooks, reels of letters, and four ledger books documenting Edward’s works.

title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
summary:
The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country

This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old.

There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service, careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation, scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold, the leisure centres closed, the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back. That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

title: Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech | John Crace
summary:
The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe

So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser.

For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never be wrong. Except when they are.

All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday?

In this film, the roar of the crowd echoing overhead through the stadium’s claustrophobic tunnels is like the wailing of the damned, while the sport’s officer class flinch and panic as if at a wartime loss. Grimly, the match was allowed to go ahead, despite the fatalities; the authorities believed the game itself would restore order on a bread-and-circuses basis, and that abandoning the match would only cause greater violence and chaos.

Heysel 85 is directed and co-written by Romanian-born and Belgian-based film-maker Teodora Ana Mihai; she is a former collaborator of Cristian Mungiu, though maybe the influence here is more Paul Greengrass. The film-makers have been criticised for fictionalising aspects: the players are depicted as not being aware that fans had died before they took to the field – they were in fact largely aware, although it may well be true that the slippery authorities sought to minimise the truth as much as they could. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes of chicory, bitter chocolate and burnt sugar.

Almost all of these products have a similar industrial imprint, uniform granules and a one-dimensional flavour profile, so they’re ultimately more a simulation of the real thing. That said, some did surprise me. At best, they taste like a cup of office filter coffee, made in a commercial drip machine and left just long enough for its aromas to fade. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site.
